query: Which material can be used for enhanced catalytic activity and durability toward HER and HOR, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Nanostructuring the surface of a high-entropy alloy (HEA) via controlled selective dealloying will enhance its catalytic activity and durability toward both hydrogen evolution (HER) and hydrogen oxidation (HOR).
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous, single-phase structure (e.g., an FCC refractory or conventional HEA) in its as-synthesized state.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled surface or interface treatment that induces selective dealloying to form a stable nanoporous surface layer.
generation.conditions: Electrochemical environments typical of fuel cells or water-splitting devices (acidic or alkaline media) under repeated cycling conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a nanoporous surface layer increases the active surface area while maintaining a robust underlying alloy framework.
generation.mechanism: The nanoporous architecture provides more active sites and improves mass transport, while the retained stability of the bulk HEA minimizes degradation under electrochemical cycling, leading to both enhanced catalytic kinetics and durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HEA is expected to exhibit lower overpotentials (improved catalytic activity) and reduced performance degradation over time (enhanced durability) relative to the non-modified HEA or conventional catalysts.
generation.baseline: Unmodified HEAs or traditional noble metal catalysts without engineered nanoporous surfaces.
generation.boundary: This approach is anticipated to be effective only for alloys that can undergo controlled, selective dealloying without losing structural integrity; excessive dealloying or inappropriate alloy compositions may compromise performance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the performance improvements (e.g., reduction in overpotential or durability gain) remains uncertain until validated by experimental data, and may depend on the specific alloy composition and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set will receive the controlled surface dealloying treatment to induce a nanoporous surface layer, and the other set will remain unmodified as a baseline. Both sets are then subjected to identical electrochemical testing under HER and HOR conditions (in either acidic or alkaline electrolyte) with repeated cycling.
measurements: Polarization curves to measure overpotential and current density for HER and HOR
Durability testing over extended cycling (monitoring performance degradation)
Morphological and compositional analysis (e.g., SEM, TEM) of the surface before and after electrochemical cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoporous surface engineered samples show no statistically significant improvement (e.g., similar or higher overpotentials, reduced current densities, or comparable degradation rates) compared to the unmodified HEA baseline, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Corrosion behavior

Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy [2] . Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion [2] .

decision.trend: None of the listed papers discusses electrocatalytic performance for hydrogen evolution or oxidation reactions, so there is no direct precedent from these references addressing the combined requirement of high activity and durability for HER/HOR. Their focus is primarily on mechanical properties, microstructural control, and radiation/thermal resistance rather than on electrochemical catalysis.
decision.unsolved: Thus far, no steps in the referenced literature have tackled the open challenge of designing a robust electrocatalyst with both high activity and durability for HER/HOR. The gap is in translating the advanced composition or microstructure strategies seen in high-entropy alloys and refractory metals research into improvements in catalytic functionality under electrochemical conditions.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled surface or interface modification (e.g., nanoporous or nanostructured surface layers) to enhance the active surface area and stability under repeated HER/HOR cycles
decision.why: Given the question’s emphasis on high catalytic activity and durability under electrochemical cycling, refining and engineering the surface region is a direct approach. This builds on modern alloy microstructural tailoring methods but focuses on topological and chemical optimization of the catalyst surface rather than adding new elements.
